Why it's the best: A 65-inch Samsung 4K screen with HDR10+, Vision AI Companion and eARC at the lowest price here

A 65-inch TV is the size many Indian homes move to once a 55-inch screen starts to feel small from the sofa. It fills a living room wall, it brings a Test match or a weekend film closer to the cinema experience, and it is also the size at which the way a screen makes its light becomes easy to see. Dark scenes, daylight from a nearby window and fast camera pans all expose those differences more clearly on a bigger panel.Samsung's 2026 range covers this size with five display technologies. The Crystal UHD sets use a standard LED backlight. The Mini LED and Neo QLED models light the picture with thousands of much smaller LEDs for tighter contrast, and the Neo QLED adds a quantum dot layer for richer colour. The new Micro RGB series goes further with separate red, green and blue LEDs behind the screen, while the OLED models do away with a backlight entirely because every pixel produces its own light. Across the six TVs here, prices run from Rs 75,990 to Rs 2,21,990.The other differences show up in daily use. Refresh rates range from 120Hz to 165Hz, which matters for anyone connecting a PlayStation 5, an Xbox Series X or a gaming PC. Built-in sound goes from 30W stereo speakers to a 70W, 4.2.2-channel system, and only the two OLEDs get Samsung's Glare Free coating for rooms with a lot of daylight. Every set runs Tizen and includes Samsung's Vision AI Companion, which brings Bixby, Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot to the TV for voice search and questions.Most OLED TVs look their best in a dark room, which is not how many Indian homes watch television. The S95H addresses that with Samsung's Glare Free coating, which cuts reflections from windows and ceiling lights while holding on to deep blacks. Each pixel still produces its own light and switches off completely for black, so a night scene in a thriller or the stands of a stadium during a day-night match keep their detail without the faint glow an LED backlight can leave around bright objects.It runs on the NQ4 AI Gen3 Processor and uses OLED HDR Pro, the top level of Samsung's OLED brightness processing. All four HDMI ports are ready for consoles and PCs, with a refresh rate of up to 165Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro, G-Sync compatibility and HGiG, so a PlayStation 5, an Xbox and a gaming PC can each keep their own input. The bigger separation from the rest of this list is sound. A 4.2.2-channel, 70W system with Object Tracking Sound+ and Dolby Atmos places drivers around the frame, so voices and effects follow the action across the screen, and many buyers will be able to skip a soundbar for everyday viewing.The FloatLayer design keeps the screen 2.64 cm deep, and the Art Store lets it display paintings when nobody is watching. It supports HDR10+ but not Dolby Vision, which, as on every Samsung TV, matters only if most of what you stream is mastered in that format. A built-in Zigbee and Thread module also allows it to work as a hub for compatible smart home devices.The S90H shares more with the S95H than the gap between them suggests. Both use the NQ4 AI Gen3 Processor, both refresh at up to 165Hz, and for 2026 Samsung has brought the Glare Free coating, once limited to its top OLED, down to the S90 series. Self-lit pixels give it the same true black and wide viewing angle, which helps in a long living room where some of the family sits well off to the side.The differences lie in brightness processing, sound and design. The S90H uses OLED HDR+ in place of HDR Pro, so the brightest highlights in HDR films do not reach the same peak as on the S95H. Its speakers are a 2.1-channel, 40W system with Object Tracking Sound Lite. That is fuller than the 30W sets further down this list and a clear step below the flagship's 70W array, though anyone planning to add a soundbar will notice the gap least, and Q-Symphony lets the TV speakers and a compatible Samsung soundbar play together.For gaming it matches the S95H feature for feature, with four HDMI ports that each accept 4K at 165Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro, G-Sync compatibility and an AI Gaming Optimizer. The LaserSlim body is 3.99 cm deep and weighs 19.1 kg without the stand.Micro RGB is Samsung's newest way of lighting an LCD screen, and the R85H is the more affordable of the two series that brought it to India this year. A conventional Mini LED TV shines white or blue light through a colour layer. The R85H instead uses tiny red, green and blue LEDs that the Micro RGB AI Engine controls on their own, so colour is produced at the backlight itself. Samsung says this covers 100% of the BT.2020 colour range, a wider standard than the DCI-P3 range most TVs are measured against.In practice the benefit shows most in bright, saturated content such as animated films, nature documentaries and the green of a cricket outfield under floodlights. Being an LCD with a backlight, it is comfortable in a well-lit room. Its blacks, however, rely on Ultimate Micro Dimming rather than pixels that switch off, so very dark scenes will not match the two OLEDs above it, and it does without the Glare Free coating Samsung reserves for the pricier R95H.Gaming support is strong, with four HDMI 2.1 ports that accept 4K at 144Hz, FreeSync Premium Pro and AI Auto Game Mode. The 2-channel, 30W speakers support Dolby Atmos and Object Tracking Sound Lite, which covers daily viewing, while films will benefit from a soundbar.The QN80H is the most balanced option here for a household that watches a bit of everything and keeps a console under the TV. It pairs a Quantum Mini LED backlight with a quantum dot layer that TÜV Rheinland certifies as Real QLED, and Samsung rates it at 100% colour volume. Colour volume is a more useful measure than colour range alone, because it tracks whether colours stay rich as the picture gets brighter, which is where ordinary LED sets lose saturation.Its Mini LEDs, managed through Supreme Mini LED Dimming, give it firmer control over dark areas than the standard backlight of the U8300H, so letterbox bars and night skies look darker in a dim room. The NQ4 AI Gen2 Processor handles upscaling, which matters in India, where most cable and DTH channels still broadcast below 4K.All four HDMI ports accept a 4K signal at 144Hz, though Samsung notes that 144Hz needs a PC graphics card, and current consoles top out at 120Hz. FreeSync Premium Pro, HGiG and ALLM are included. Sound comes from a 30W, 2-channel system with Dolby Atmos and Object Tracking Sound Lite, and the set weighs 17.2 kg without its stand.Samsung added a separate Mini LED range below its Neo QLED sets this year, and the M80H sits at the top of it. Like the QN80H, it lights the screen with Mini LEDs and controls them through Supreme Mini LED Dimming. It does without the quantum dot layer and Real QLED certification, using Samsung's Pure Spectrum Color processing instead, so the main difference between the two is how well colours hold up in very bright scenes.Much of the rest carries over. The M80H has the same NQ4 AI Gen2 Processor, the same Motion Xcelerator 144Hz, AI Auto Game Mode and HGiG. Two details matter for gamers: there are three HDMI ports instead of four, and it supports FreeSync Premium instead of Premium Pro, which leaves out AMD's HDR gaming certification. Someone with one console and a set-top box will rarely feel either.It weighs 14.6 kg without the stand, takes a 200 x 200 mm wall mount and draws 101W in typical use. The 30W, 2-channel speakers include Object Tracking Sound Lite and Q-Symphony, and Samsung promises seven years of Tizen OS upgrades on the range.For many buyers, the move to 65 inches is about screen size first and display technology second, and the U8300H is built around that priority. It uses a standard LED backlight with Samsung's Crystal Processor 4K and HDR10+, and it carries the same Vision AI Companion as the sets above it, so Bixby, Perplexity and Microsoft Copilot are available from the remote.It shares its body size with the M80H, and the differences sit in the backlight and motion handling. Without Mini LEDs, contrast relies on Mega Contrast processing, so dark scenes watched with the lights off look greyer than on any other TV in this list. Its refresh rate is listed as DLG 120Hz, a mode that doubles the frame rate by lowering vertical resolution. ALLM and VRR are supported, which suits casual console gaming more than competitive play.Sound comes from 30W, 2-channel speakers with Object Tracking Sound Lite. There are three HDMI ports, one with eARC for a soundbar, and a single USB port. Samsung TV Plus is built in, and the Football Mode preset adjusts picture and sound for live sport.
Article Summary: summarize: ​Best Samsung 65-inch 4K smart TV in India. Samsung OLED S95H, OLED S90H, Micro RGB R85H, Neo QLED QN80H, Mini LED M80H and Crystal UHD U8300H: Specifications at a glance.

Article Title: A colourful walk down Delhi’s Said-ul-Ajaib lane
Article Text:
One of the remaining old structures, a haveli has been chosen as the exhibition venue (Photo credit: Anushka Kogta)

The artwork portrays the village's transition from its historical roots to modern developments (Photo credit: Anushka Kogta)

The initiative is aimed at fostering a sense of belonging among residents regarding their cultural heritage (Photo credit: Anushka Kogta)

Local artists use photographs to paint familiar scenes on walls in the neighborhood (Photo credit: Anushka Kogta)

Students from Dr BR Ambedkar University Delhi are creating an exhibition to showcase the history of Said-ul-Ajaib (Photo credit: Anushka Kogta)





NEW DELHI: Along the narrow lanes leading to a crumbling haveli in Said-ul-Ajaib, artists are painting scenes and familiar features from the neighbourhood on the walls.Old doorways and architectural details sit alongside illustrations of a tree, a water structure, people and cattle, as well as colourful depictions of everyday life. The paintings, based on photographs taken in and around the neighbourhood, are part of an exhibition that will explore Said-ul-Ajaib’s history and heritage.Titled Sanjha Said-ul-Ajaib—with sanjha meaning ‘ours’- the exhibition is organised by students of Dr BR Ambedkar University Delhi as part of their Urban Studies Studio course.Led by assistant professor Dr Shekhar Tokas and associate professor Dr Nidhi Tewathia, the students have documented the village through five themes: history, heritage, culture, disaster and risk and gully intervention. Their work also covers gender, economy, and changing livelihoods through photographs, maps, paintings and interviews.For Tokas, the idea is to bring Delhi’s villages into discussions about the city’s history. While Delhi is known for its monuments and seven historical cities, its villages rarely get the same attention. “These are villages older than Delhi, and they have a contribution,” he says.Over the years, Said-ul-Ajaib’s landscape has changed considerably.Sanjay Tewatia, 53, whose amily has lived here for seven or eight generations, remembers a very different place. “Earlier, there were only 30-40 houses. There were fields and a forest. We used to play in the fields. There were date palms and mango trees,” he recalls.Today, multi-storey buildings stand in their place, and two of the three old havelis he remembers have been torn down.One of the remaining old structures, a haveli has been chosen as the exhibition venue. The building has been left largely in its existing condition, rather than being extensively renovated.Atishay Khanna, who is leading the design intervention at Said-ul-Ajaib, says that holding the show in an old structure surrounded by apartments reminds people of the village’s roots. The idea, he says, is to create a sense of belonging and encourage residents to take ownership of the spaces they inhabit.The work in the lanes is another part of this effort.Suhani, 23, is using white cement and paint to recreate photographs taken around Said-ul-Ajaib. The paintings include familiar landmarks as well as details of older architecture.“We took pictures and then drew them here. We want to show the transition from historical times to modern times,” she says.
Article Summary: Students from Dr BR Ambedkar University Delhi are creating an exhibition to showcase the history of Said-ul-Ajaib. The initiative is aimed at fostering a sense of belonging among residents regarding their cultural heritage. The paintings include familiar landmarks as well as details of older architecture.

Article Title: LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero has a tip for Gen Z job seekers: Talk to someone who already…
Article Text:
LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero

LinkedIn CEO: AI is making the entry-level job market tougher

LinkedIn CEO says networking can be the fastest way to get a job

Why companies are hiring Gen Z for AI skills

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

AI is changing the job market, making it harder for fresh graduates to find entry-level jobs. But LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero believes Gen Z could also have an advantage as companies look for people who understand how to use AI at work. His advice to young job seekers, however, goes beyond learning new technology or sending out more applications. In an interview with Fortune recently, LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero said that building professional connections could be the fastest way to get hired. Instead of simply applying for jobs online, graduates should try to speak to someone already working at the company they want to join.Daniel Shapero described the current employment situation as a “frozen” job market, saying it is particularly difficult for people at the beginning of their careers. “It is a frozen job market, and that does make it tougher for people that are earlier in their career for sure,” Shapero told Fortune.However, he believes young candidates may have an advantage during job interviews as companies increasingly adopt artificial intelligence. Employers are looking for people who can understand new technology and use it to change the way businesses work.“There is a belief that people that are earlier, maybe they’re more attuned to the latest tech, and they understand how to use AI in their job,” Shapero said.He added that companies want to hire people who can help them “transform how the company operates.”This could create opportunities for Gen Z candidates, even as AI tools change the kind of work companies expect employees to do.Apart from building AI skills, Daniel Shapero has another suggestion for Gen Z job seekers: do not depend only on online applications. According to LinkedIn's data, the “fastest path” to landing a job is connecting with someone who already works at the company where a candidate wants to apply.This means reaching out to employees, building professional relationships and asking for introductions could be more useful than simply sending applications and waiting for a response. Shapero compared the job search process to raising money for a startup. Founders do not simply send emails to investors and hope someone agrees to fund their business. They try to meet people and build connections that can lead to introductions.“You wouldn’t just email all the VCs and hope that someone wrote you a check,” he said. “You would try to meet people. You would try to have those people introduce you to others.”His advice suggests that job seekers should approach their search in a similar way. Instead of relying entirely on application portals, they can identify people working in their target companies, start conversations and learn more about available opportunities.LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero is not the only business leader who believes younger workers could bring an advantage to companies adopting AI. Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise, a generative AI platform, said he is actively hiring entry-level candidates because they are more open to experimenting with new technology.“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries… They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities,” Chen told Fortune.He also believes younger employees can bring fresh thinking to businesses. “And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”The growing demand for AI-related skills could therefore give fresh graduates opportunities beyond traditional entry-level roles. Shapero also advised young candidates to consider jobs in industries they may not have initially thought about.“Sometimes your degree or your skills can be applied in areas that you maybe haven’t thought of,” he said adding “These days every company is a bit of a tech company.”
Article Summary: LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero believes Gen Z could have an advantage as companies look for people who understand how to use AI at work. His advice to young job seekers goes beyond learning new technology or sending out more applications. Instead of simply applying for jobs online, graduates should try to speak to someone already working at the company.

Article Title: Government’s anti-cybercrime wing has ‘WhatsApp Web’ warning for you
Article Text:
Whatsapp Web

‘Closing the browser tab is not enough’

Key safety tips from advisory

Avoid logging into WhatsApp Web on cyber cafe computers, public kiosks, hotel business centers, borrowed laptops or other unknown and public devices.

If logging in on a shared system is unavoidable, use the browser’s incognito or private browsing mode but remember to log out manually afterward.

Pay close attention to unusual account behaviour, such as unexpected messages sent from your number, strange replies from contacts or any unexplained activity.

Keep your devices, operating systems, browsers and security software updated, and steer clear of suspicious downloads, unknown files and cracked software.

The government’s anti-cybercrime wing has issued a warning for those who use WhatsApp Web . In a new security advisory issued on Monday (November 23), the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) cautioned that active, authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions can be exploited for unauthorised access by hackers by leaving an open door to hijack your account, read private chats and impersonate you to carry out fraud,Once inside, bad actors can read personal messages, view contact lists and group chats, and send messages pretending to be the account owner, leveraging the victim's trusted identity to launch fraud, phishing, and social-engineering scams, the warning explained as per PTI.The I4C specifically stressed that simply closing a browser window or tab does not end a WhatsApp Web session. Users must manually log out every time they finish using the platform on a computer.“Users are therefore advised to exercise caution while using WhatsApp Web, particularly on office computers, shared systems, public computers or devices that may be accessible to other persons," the advisory stated, further warning, “Avoid official or sensitive work on WhatsApp Web. Government, organisational, financial, confidential or other sensitive information should preferably not be exchanged through WhatsApp Web sessions on computers. ”To protect accounts from unauthorised takeovers, the I4C recommended the following precautions:
Article Summary: The government’s anti-cybercrime wing has issued a warning for those who use WhatsApp Web. The National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU) under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) cautioned that active, authenticated WhatsApp Web sessions can be exploited by hackers.

Article Title: Educators, librarians to discuss AI’s role in future of learning
Article Text:

Article Title: Punawadi Festival to showcase Pune’s historical and cultural journey from January 10
Article Text:
Punawadi Festival to showcase Pune’s historical and cultural journey from Jan 10

Pune:





The eight-day ‘Punawadi Festival 2026’, showcasing the journey of Pune from its ancient name Punawadi to the present-day historic and modern city, will be held from Jan 10 to 17 at Pu La Deshpande Kalagram on Sinhagad Road in Pune.The festival is being jointly organised by Sadaiv Foundation and Hanuman Mitra Mandal, Kasba Peth, with the theme ‘Historical Heritage, Aspirations for Modernity’.The event aims to showcase Pune’s historical, literary and cultural heritage through exhibitions, performances and interactive activities.Announcing the festival at a news conference, Aniruddha Yewale, trustee of Sadaiv Foundation and chief organiser of the festival, said a replica of old Pune would be created across 4.5 acres, offering visitors a glimpse of the city’s traditional lifestyle, art, culture and festivals. The organisers plan to make it an annual public festival.Former MLA Ulhas Pawar said the initiative would help introduce Pune’s historical, cultural, literary and artistic legacy to the younger generation. Artist Sharadchandra Tarde stressed the need for collective efforts to preserve the city’s artistic and cultural traditions.The festival will feature performances of theatre, Dhol-Tasha, sword fighting, spear throwing, kabaddi and kho-kho.Around 10,000 students and more than 300 artists are expected to participate, said Parag Thakur. A dedicated technology pavilion showcasing Pune’s research and technological developments, including artificial intelligence, has also been proposed by IT expert Dr Deepak Shikarpurkar.The cultural section will include presentations of the Peshwa court, Maratha-era warriors, a freedom fighters’ gallery, Mangalagaur games, Bharud, Powada, Gondhal and Lavani. Visitors will also be able to experience Shaniwar Wada through virtual reality and explore Pune’s history using artificial intelligence.Traditional art forms such as Warli painting, Paithani weaving and Tambat Ali handicrafts will be showcased alongside AI art, digital paintings and 3D installations.Happiness coach Makarand Tillu said members of Navchaitanya Hasya Parivar would present a laughter yoga programme at the inaugural ceremony. The organisation has 250 laughter clubs and around 25,000 members, he added.Mahesh Suryawanshi, Milind Ladge, Suryakant Pathak, Prof. Dr Charudatta Aphale, Dr Sanjay Upadhye, Prof. Milind Joshi, Acharya Shahir Hemant Raje Mavale, Anand Saraf and several representatives from social, cultural and educational organisations were present at the news conference.The organisers have appealed to citizens and visitors to attend the festival and experience the city’s historical legacy, traditional arts, cultural practices and modern innovations.
Article Summary: The eight-day ‘Punawadi Festival 2026’ will be held from Jan 10 to 17 at Pu La Deshpande Kalagram on Sinhagad Road in Pune. The event aims to showcase Pune’s historical, literary and cultural heritage through exhibitions, performances and interactive activities.

Article Title: Rotterdam built a public square that turns into a giant rainwater reservoir during heavy downpours; when the weather is dry, its basins become basketball and volleyball courts
Article Text:
The Water Square Benthemplein. Image Credit: Landezine

How Rotterdam's water square stores rainwater during heavy downpours

Three basins manage different levels of rainfall

The square is also useful when there is no rain

Local residents helped shape the design

Rotterdam has expanded the water square concept

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Rotterdam has found a unique way to deal with heavy rainfall by turning a public square into a temporary water storage space that also serves as a recreational area. The Water Square Benthemplein, designed by Dutch architecture firm De Urbanisten, collects rainwater during downpours and holds it in specially designed basins. During the dry season, the same area becomes a place for residents to play basketball, volleyball and other sports, demonstrating how urban infrastructure can serve more than one purpose.The Water Square Benthemplein was created to address a problem that Rotterdam has faced during intense rainfall. When large amounts of rain fall within a short period, parts of the city can flood because the existing water system cannot always process the additional water quickly enough.The Climate Adaptation Platform Netherlands says that the concept of water squares is to give residential areas places where rainwater can be collected and released in a controlled way. Instead of letting too much water overwhelm the drainage system, specially designed public spaces temporarily hold the water until the city’s water infrastructure can handle it.Benthemplein is one of the most prominent examples of this approach.The square has a storage capacity of 1,800 cubic metres, making it a significant part of Rotterdam's efforts to manage heavy rainfall. Its design also ensures that the space remains useful to residents when there is no immediate need to store water.The project was designed by De Urbanisten and officially opened on 4 December 2013, according to Landezine's project profile.One of the most important features of Benthemplein is its 3 separate water basins. According to the Dutch Architects, 2 shallow basins collect rainwater from the immediate surroundings whenever it rains. A third, deeper basin is designed to receive water when rainfall continues for longer and larger quantities need to be stored.The water reaches these basins through large stainless-steel gutters that run across the square. The design also includes a water wall and a rain well, which make the movement of rainwater visible to people visiting the space. The water wall directs rainfall towards the deeper basin, while the rain well brings water from a neighbouring building into the gutter system.De Urbanisten explains that the water is gradually channelled into the square rather than being allowed to collect unpredictably. The design also accounts for what happens after the rain stops. According to Dutch Architects, water collected in the shallow basins moves into an underground infiltration system, allowing it to gradually seep into the groundwater. This helps maintain groundwater levels and supports nearby trees and plants, particularly during dry periods.Water from the deeper basin is returned to Rotterdam's open-water system within a maximum of 36 hours. This arrangement also prevents all the collected rainwater from immediately entering the city's combined sewage system.The water square was never intended to function only as a flood-control facility. Its designers wanted to create a lively neighbourhood destination that residents could enjoy throughout the year.When the basins are dry, the deeper section becomes a sports area where visitors can play basketball, football and volleyball. The stepped edges around the basin also provide seating, allowing spectators to watch games or simply spend time with others.The shallower sections have different recreational uses. One is designed for skating and other activities on wheels, while another includes a smooth surface intended for dancing and informal gatherings. The surrounding areas feature trees, ornamental grasses and flowers, creating quieter places for people who prefer to sit and relax.Landezine's project description highlights how the square combines sports facilities, greenery and water management without making the recreational areas feel like secondary additions. The design uses different shades of blue on surfaces that can hold water, while stainless steel marks the structures that transport it. This makes the square's water-management purpose visible even during dry weather.According to Dutch Architects, students and teachers from Zadkine College and the Graphic Lyceum, members of a nearby church, a youth theatre, a gym and local residents participated in the planning process.Three workshops were organised to discuss how the square should look, what activities it should accommodate and how rainwater could become part of the experience. Participants wanted a place that offered plenty of room for young people while also providing green and quieter areas for relaxation.The German Development Institute's 2021 paper explains that the consultation process took place over 6 months and focused on activities, design choices and refining the ideas proposed by participants. The paper notes that the workshops shaped features such as the basketball area, skating facilities and seating arrangements.Benthemplein is not the only public space of its kind in Rotterdam. The city has developed smaller water squares in other neighbourhoods as part of its wider approach to managing rainfall.According to the Climate Adaptation Platform Netherlands, Bellamy Square in Spangen includes a water-storage section with a capacity of 250 cubic metres. Another example is Kleinpolder Square in Overschie, where an underground basin collects overflow water from nearby surface water. The space also accommodates public sculptures placed on raised platforms to protect them from flooding.Benthemplein’s large storage capacity also made the construction more expensive. Piling work was required during construction, while funding included support from the Dutch government's Beautiful Netherlands Innovation Programme and an INTERREG subsidy from the European Union.De Urbanisten's research into water squares began in 2006-2007, and the concept became part of Rotterdam's official urban policy through Rotterdam Waterplan 2 in 2007.
Article Summary: The Water Square Benthemplein collects rainwater during downpours and holds it in specially designed basins. During the dry season, the same area becomes a place for residents to play basketball, volleyball and other sports. The square has a storage capacity of 1,800 cubic metres and was designed by Dutch architecture firm De Urbanisten.

Article Title: After Etsy changed its terms to permit AI training using sellers' content, longtime artists began shutting their online shops; the company has now promised to rewrite the policy following the backlash
Article Text:
Etsy sellers shut shops over revised terms allowing their work to be used for AI training. AI image

Artists shut shops after policy change

Etsy says it will protect human creativity

Etsy has faced seller protests before

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Several longtime sellers on Etsy have started closing their online shops after the marketplace introduced new terms allowing sellers' content to be used for artificial intelligence (AI) development. The decision has upset artists and small business owners, who fear their original work could be used by AI companies without their permission.The revised terms, which are scheduled to take effect on December 16, allow Etsy and its "third party partners and vendors" to use sellers' content to develop, train, test and improve AI and machine learning technologies. The company says these tools will help improve the marketplace and make it safer for users.However, sellers are concerned about the broad permission given to outside companies. According to The Inquirer, some have decided to leave a platform they had used for years rather than accept the new conditions. Following the protests, Etsy has promised to rewrite the policy and provide a clearer explanation of how sellers' work may be used.Illustrator Aaron Millard was among those who decided to leave. He announced on Instagram last week that he was deleting the Etsy shop he had operated for nearly a decade.Millard objected to the possibility of his artwork being used to train AI systems and shared with third parties. He also criticised the absence of an option for sellers to refuse such use. "My work took years to learn and create. I won’t let it be stolen," he wrote.Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus, founders of home goods and stationery brand Cognitive Surplus, also removed their shop after selling through Etsy for 13 years. In an Instagram post last Thursday, they criticised the company's approach to sellers' creative work and the possibility of third parties benefiting from it.Kristen Zephyrus explained their decision in an interview on Friday. "For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful," she said. "We don’t want anything to do with that."Etsy has defended the revised policy, saying the intention is not to use artists' work to reproduce their creations through AI.James Ossman, the company's vice president for customer operations, addressed sellers in a statement published on Etsy's website earlier this week. He said the company would not use their content to train AI models designed to copy original work or replace human creativity.Ossman cited fraud detection tools and advertising on the platform as reasons for allowing third parties to access sellers' content.However, the explanation has not prevented criticism of the revised terms. Sellers remain concerned about the extent of permission being granted and how their work could be used outside the marketplace.In an email to The New York Times on Friday, Ossman said Etsy was working to make the wording clearer and would share revised terms directly with sellers soon."We’ve heard sellers’ concerns about the updated terms, and we should have done more to explain how we use their content to help buyers discover their work, support their businesses and keep Etsy safe," he wrote.He also stressed that creators retained ownership of their work, adding, "Their creative work belongs to them."Founded in 2005, Etsy was created to help independent artisans find customers online. However, disagreements over company policies have previously led to protests from its seller community.In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike after Etsy increased its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%, marking a 30% rise.The company also faced complaints in October over the growing presence of low-quality AI-generated content, commonly described by users as "AI slop". Etsy subsequently announced tighter restrictions on such material.The latest dispute comes as several internet companies face pressure to adopt AI while dealing with concerns from users who oppose the technology's use. A Gallup poll conducted during the summer found that nearly 40% of Americans believed AI did more harm than good.
Article Summary: Etsy has introduced new terms allowing sellers' content to be used for AI development. The decision has upset artists and small business owners, who fear their original work could be used by AI companies without their permission. Etsy has promised to rewrite the policy and provide a clearer explanation.

Article Title: Australia planted trees across 255 farmland sites to restore habitats; 12 years later, scientists found bird communities moving towards native woodland but still not fully resembling natural habitats
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How did 12 years of farmland restoration change bird communities in Australia

What did bird surveys reveal about Australia's farmland restoration

Bird communities in restored Australian farmland moved closer to native woodland

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why did livestock exclusion matter for bird communities

Australia's farmland restoration efforts have helped bird communities move closer to those found in native woodland, but the changes have not been enough to restore their original composition. Researchers examined 255 sites in south-west Victoria, comparing farmland, revegetation plantings and areas of remnant native vegetation. The study examined changes recorded over a 12-year period, using bird surveys conducted in 2006/2007 and 2019.According to research published in the journal Ecological Applications, titled ‘ Temporal dynamics in the composition of bird communities along a gradient of farmland restoration ’, bird communities in restored areas became less similar to those in unrestored farmland and more similar to those in native vegetation. However, the plantings had not fully replicated the bird communities found in natural habitats, even after several decades of growth.The study covered a heavily cleared agricultural region in south-west Victoria, where more than 90% of the agricultural region had been removed. Researchers selected 23 landscapes, each covering 800 hectares, and surveyed birds across farmland, revegetation plantings and remnant native vegetation.The sites represented different stages of restoration, including plantings aged between 2 and 40 years during the first survey period in 2006/2007. By 2019, those plantings were between 14 and 52 years old. The researchers retained 255 sites for analysis after excluding locations affected by access problems, land-use changes, pine plantations, and wetlands. The sites included 47 native vegetation, 73 revegetation plantings, 63 scattered paddock trees and 75 open pasture, 2 pine plantations, and 16 wetlands/dams.Bird surveys took place in 2006/2007 and again in 2019, allowing researchers to examine changes across 12 years. At each site, an observer spent 15 minutes searching a one-hectare area for birds. Every site was surveyed four times, with visits spread across the seasons and divided between mornings and afternoons. Researchers recorded species seen or heard during the surveys and compared the bird communities associated with different habitat types.The analysis considered all land birds as well as woodland birds, which rely on native vegetation for breeding and feeding. Water birds and exotic species were excluded. The researchers assessed changes in community composition, rather than relying only on species numbers.The results showed that each habitat type supported a distinct bird community. Over the 12 years, bird assemblages in revegetation plantings moved away from those found in unrestored farmland and towards those in remnant native vegetation. The researchers also found that plantings supported richer and more diverse bird assemblages than unrestored farmland.They added a distinct bird community to rural landscapes, increasing the overall diversity of habitats available to birds. The study found that revegetation plantings had not replicated reference habitats even after approximately 40 to 50 years, showing that changes in bird community composition can take much longer.Two features of the surrounding landscape and planting management were linked to greater changes in bird communities. Plantings were more likely to move away from the bird assemblages found in unrestored farmland when they were located in areas with greater surrounding tree cover. They were also more likely to show this shift when livestock were mostly excluded, compared with grazed plantings.Complete convergence with reference habitats could take centuries in the study region. Their findings point to the importance of protecting existing natural and semi-natural habitats alongside restoration work. They also have implications for environmental offset programmes, which need to account for the long timescales involved in rebuilding ecological communities.
Article Summary: Researchers examined 255 sites in south-west Victoria, comparing farmland, revegetation plantings and areas of remnant native vegetation. Study examined changes recorded over a 12-year period, using bird surveys conducted in 2006/2007 and 2019. Plantings had not fully replicated the bird communities found in natural habitats, even after decades of growth.

Article Title: Musk's SpaceXSI denies liability over Grok-generated sexualised images of UK lawmaker
Article Text:
SpaceXSI also denied violating her data protection rights. It argued that it 'did not determine the content of the relevant users' prompts'

'Fictitious and implausible'

Lawmaker challenges company's defence

A test case for AI companies

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Grok faces scrutiny across countries

Elon Musk's SpaceX Super Intelligence (SpaceXSI) has denied legal responsibility for fake sexualised images of a British lawmaker generated using its Grok AI platform. In a written defence filed at London's High Court on October 29, the company argued that AI-generated images that are obviously fictitious cannot violate a person's right to privacy. The response came in a lawsuit filed by Jess Asato, a member of Britain's governing Labour Party, who is seeking an order to prevent Grok from creating manipulated images of her.SpaceXSI has denied allegations of misuse of private information and breaches of data protection laws. It has also contested Asato's request for an order requiring it to "implement effective and permanent technical measures" to stop Grok from generating manipulated images of her.In its defence, lawyers for SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC said the company had removed AI-generated images of Asato that violated its terms. These included a video showing her "being chloroformed and prepared for a sexual assault".However, the company argued that other images it had allowed to remain online were clearly artificial.They said such content "would be understood by reasonable and sensible persons viewing that content to be AI-generated, fictitious and implausible ...rather than as realistic images".On this basis, the company argued that Asato could not claim a reasonable expectation of privacy.SpaceXSI also denied violating her data protection rights. It argued that it "did not determine the content of the relevant users' prompts".Asato hit back at the company's position on Thursday, saying that developers of powerful AI tools must be held accountable for their products."SpaceX SI wants to have it both ways," she said."The company admits it built the AI model, rewrote user requests to add its own graphic details, pulled images from across the internet, and published the results from an account it controls," she said, adding: "Yet it also claims it is a neutral bystander without legal responsibility".Asato has accused the company of designing and training Grok in a way that enabled users to generate sexualised images of her. Her lawsuit alleges misuse of private information and breaches of data protection laws.The lawsuit is among the first cases to examine whether an AI developer can be held legally responsible for the way its system is designed and the content it generates.The court's eventual findings could have implications for similar cases involving AI-generated content and the responsibilities of companies developing such tools.Grok, which is available through Musk's social media platform X, has faced regulatory scrutiny in several countries following an outcry over its use to generate sexualised images of people without their consent.In mid-January, xAI said it had restricted image editing on Grok. It also said it had blocked users from generating images of people in revealing clothing "where it's illegal".However, a Reuters investigation in early February found that Grok continued to generate sexualised images even after the restrictions were introduced. The platform did so even when users explicitly warned that the people depicted had not consented.In July, xAI sued a man in the US, alleging that he had misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material. The case was among the first of its kind brought by an AI company.
Article Summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX Super Intelligence (SpaceXSI) has denied legal responsibility for fake sexualised images of a British lawmaker generated using its Grok AI platform. The company argued that AI-generated images that are obviously fictitious cannot violate a person's right to privacy. The response came in a lawsuit filed by Jess Asato, a member of Britain's governing Labour Party.

Article Title: Meet 16-year-old Anisha Dhoot, student from Oregon, who combined seaweed fertiliser, plastic-waste biochar and AI trained on 17,000 environmental data points to develop a farming tool with 99% accurac
Article Text:
Anisha Dhoot. Image Credit: Barron Prize/Website

How Anisha Dhoot combined seaweed fertiliser , plastic-waste biochar and AI

What makes her EARTH-ai farming tool different

How did a teenager learn to build an AI model

Her work is aimed at helping small-scale farmers

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Recognition has helped bring attention to her environmental work

A 16-year-old student from Oregon has developed an agricultural innovation that brings together seaweed-based fertiliser, recycled plastic waste and artificial intelligence to address some of farming’s biggest challenges. Anisha Dhoot’s project, called Smart Carbon Recycling, aims to improve damaged soil, support healthier crop growth and help farmers make better decisions about what to plant. Her work combines a low-cost biofertiliser with a machine learning model that analyses environmental conditions and predicts suitable crops, offering a potential solution for farmers dealing with changing climates and declining soil quality.According to the Gloria Barron Prize website, Dhoot developed Smart Carbon Recycling as a way to connect sustainable agriculture with climate action. The project brings together three main elements: seaweed-based fertiliser, biochar made from waste materials and an artificial intelligence system designed to guide crop selection.Her first major development was KelpNutriBoost, a biofertiliser made using kelp collected from the Oregon coast.Dhoot recognised the potential of seaweed as a useful agricultural resource because of its ability to support soil quality and contribute to carbon storage.Kelp grows quickly and can capture carbon from the atmosphere. Dhoot explored how this natural resource could be turned into an affordable product that helps farmers improve soil conditions while supporting more sustainable food production.The project later expanded beyond seaweed. She incorporated carbon-rich biochar produced from recycled plastic waste and sewage treatment plant biosolids. According to the Barron Prize, this combination was designed to improve soil fertility, plant growth rates and the nutritional quality of crops.Alongside developing the fertiliser, Dhoot recognised that farmers also needed better information when deciding which crops to grow. Soil conditions and local weather patterns can influence whether a particular crop performs well, making agricultural planning difficult, particularly in areas experiencing environmental changes.She then began developing a machine learning model that could study environmental information and identify crops suited to particular locations.The Barron Prize website states that Dhoot trained her model using a publicly available dataset containing 17,000 environmental parameters. The system analyses local soil and climate conditions to predict which crops are most likely to grow successfully.She named the tool EARTH-ai, which stands for Environmentally Aware Revolutionary Technique for Harvesting.The model reportedly achieves 99% predictive accuracy, making it one of the most notable parts of her agricultural project. It also features a smartphone-friendly interface, allowing farmers to access its recommendations without needing complicated computer systems.Rather than relying entirely on traditional methods or guesswork, the tool aims to give farmers additional information before they decide what to plant.Dhoot's achievement also involved learning several technical skills independently. According to the Barron Prize, she taught herself coding through online courses, including a Python programming course led by an MIT professor.She did not begin with all the technical knowledge required to build the system. Instead, she worked towards understanding how programming and machine learning could be used to address an environmental problem.Although the project involves artificial intelligence and advanced material development, its intended users include small-scale farmers who may not have access to expensive agricultural technologies.The Barron Prize explains that Smart Carbon Recycling is designed to provide farmers, particularly those in developing countries, with a strategy for more climate-friendly agriculture.Soil degradation and food insecurity remain important challenges in many agricultural communities. Deteriorating soil conditions can affect crop productivity, while changing environmental conditions make it harder for farmers to decide which crops are suitable for their land. KelpNutriBoost and biochar are intended to improve soil quality, while EARTH-ai offers information to help farmers select suitable crops.Dhoot's efforts received national recognition when she was named a 2025 recipient of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes.The award recognises young people between the ages of 8 and 18 who have made a significant positive contribution to people or the environment. According to Biochar Today, the prize includes a $10,000 grant to support her initiatives.Beyond developing the technology and fertiliser, she has also worked to bring her ideas into local communities. The Barron Prize reports that she distributes her kelp-based fertiliser to farming communities, organises educational activities and supports fundraising efforts for the Oregon Food Bank.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.

Article Title: Instagram tests 90-minute horizontal videos - what it means for long-form content creators

Instagram on Monday began testing new features, including 90-minute horizontal videos to target long-form content creators like podcasters and comedians, with select creators in the US.The feature, called “Features”, will allow them to link short reel clips, typically around three minutes or less, to full-length videos, as per The Hollywood Reporter.“What you’re now going to be able to do is, you see a clip of a podcast that you love, you can just click and continue watching or watch the full video, and you’ll be able to dive in and see the whole thing because creators are going to be able to link these Reels to their overall feature,” vice-president of product at Instagram, Tessa Lyons, said.Instagram has already been testing Features with creators in Brazil and plans to expand the trial to tens of thousands of creators in the US. The videos will reportedly be recommended to users through the Explore page and other areas of the platform.The feature will be available on mobile, with Instagram aiming to extend the viewing experience to its TV app. Instagram for TV, which launched last year and is available on Samsung , Fire TV and Google TV, is now expanding to Apple TV in the US.“We think the best viewing experience for longform horizontal content is on a big, horizontal screen, and so I think that is where we will expect a lot of the deep consumption to happen over time,” Lyons said, as per The Hollywood Reporter.Instagram is also experimenting with “Series”, a feature that gives episodic Reels a dedicated space on a creator’s profile. The move comes amid growing interest in microdramas and episodic videos among creators.In June, the company began reaching out to microdrama studios in Southeast Asia to test the feature. It has since approached individual creators who have been experimenting with episodic content.Instagram plans to begin testing Series in more countries in the coming months, with a US launch targeted for the end of this year or early next year. Article Title: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff admits there is no one pricing model, explains 6 ways how AI is changing software sales
Article Text:
Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff

The 6 ways AI is changing software pricing

Named users: Traditional per-user, per-month billing remains a major pillar of the software industry – much like paying a monthly per-seat fee for tools such as Claude or OpenAI.

Named agents: As AI agents take on independent workloads, companies can pay based on each individual AI agent deployed.

Usage: Customers are billed according to how actively they use the product.

Consumption: Billing is tied directly to the volume of resources consumed, which can include AI tokens or data storage.

Transaction outcomes: Payment is triggered when a specific action is finished, meaning the software vendor gets paid because a transaction was completed.

Business outcomes: The last model, which is the most results-driven tier, ties pricing directly to financial impact, where the vendor takes a percentage of the money saved or the new revenue generated for the client.

Custom agreements for a $50 billion business

Poll Vote & Share your view Which sales pricing model do you think will dominate the AI era? Named users Named agents Business outcomes 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff says the days of relying on a single billing formula for sales are over even as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes enterprise software. He explained that there is no single “perfect pricing mechanism” that works for every customer, unlike previously where companies followed the ‘traditional’ Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) and IT services business models. Earlier this year, there were fears that autonomous AI agents and AI-driven coding could disrupt workflows, eliminating the need for software platforms. When asked whether Salesforce can actually deliver outcome-based pricing in the AI era, Benioff broke down how software sales are evolving across six distinct pricing dimensions.Benioff said Salesforce is projected to bring in more than $50 billion next year, while noting that the company cannot afford to lock itself into just one pricing model and must instead offer custom agreements tailored to each client.According to Benioff, enterprise software pricing now spans six different approaches: Named users, named Agents, usage, consumption, transactions, and business outcomes.“Well, right now, number one. There is no perfect pricing mechanism for all customers. So I look at it on 6 dimensions. ‘Named users’ is still a major aspect of our industry. I'm sure you have either Claude or OpenAI, and you pay a per user price per user per month.Named Agents. So, you're paying by the agent. I think number three is usage. I've used so much of the product. Number four might be consumption. I consumed so much. That could also be tokens that could be storage. Number five is going to be outcomes or transaction outcomes. I completed the transaction, therefore I'm paid. And the final one is business outcomes. I saved you so much money. I want a percentage of that, or I made you so much money. I want a percentage of that,” Benioff said on the Sources Podcast.Asked whether Salesforce plans to offer every single one of those models, Benioff confirmed that the company's scale demands total flexibility.“Well, with our size, we’re going to do more than 50 billion dollars next year. We cannot be limited by one pricing model,” Benioff said, adding, “We have to do users, agents, consumption, usage, transactions and business. We have to do all of it for our customers. We're willing to write with them a custom agreement to say this is the perfect agreement for you.”Last year in November, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hinted at this change on Dwarkesh Podcast that the company’s pricing model is going to change. Nadella revealed the company is shifting from charging “per user” to “per agent” as AI systems increasingly perform autonomous work alongside human employees.Nadella said: “Our business, which today is an end-user tools business, will become essentially an infrastructure business in support of agents doing work. The way to think about the per-user business is not just per user, it's per agent.”
Article Summary: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff says the days of relying on a single billing formula for sales are over. He explained that there is no single ‘perfect pricing mechanism’ that works for every customer, unlike previously where companies followed the ‘traditional’ Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) and IT services business models.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says, ‘What machines did to weavers, AI is starting to do to…’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

'What machines did to weavers, AI is starting to do to mathematicians and programmers'

AI lowers barriers to specialised work

Agreeing with a professor’s essay

Read Sridhar Vembu’s complete post here

"The intellectual class never quite experienced the loss of purpose in their lives that many other classes of humans experienced. And this explains the heightened written angst.."

I agree with Prof Subbarao, who has done a lot of work in evaluating AI capability.

Yesterday, I personally prompted AI to optimize a piece of code in about an hour (while I was on the road) that would have easily taken a very smart programmer at least a month to do.

It was not an easy piece of code at all and AI understood my high level intent very clearly and came up with a detailed plan and cleanly executed it and tested it against very detailed and exhaustive test cases it had constructed itself.

The whole thing cost about $4 in tokens.

And also yesterday, one of my non-technical colleagues showed me how he used his personal AI account to do the detailed mechanical CAD design for a motor housing, and the AI used a newly released low cost CAD software he had in his machine, which I doubt the AI was trained on.

He has no engineering background, but has a curious and active mind.

What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers and ...

On the positive side, the example of my non-technical colleague shows how AI can enable a curious and active mind to explore realms he could not imagine doing before AI.

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has drawn parallels between the impact of artificial intelligence on knowledge workers and the effect mechanisation had on traditional craftsmen during the industrial revolution, warning that AI beginning to transform professions once considered safe from automation. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Vembu wrote that recent advances in AI have demonstrated capabilities which can dramatically reduce the time and expertise needed for tasks ranging from software development to engineering design. He also emphasised that the disruption is now reaching programmers, mathematicians and other intellectual professions mirrors what farmers, weavers, carpenters and ironsmiths experienced during earlier waves of industrialisation.Vembu said he recently used AI to optimise a complex piece of software code while travelling, a task he believes would have taken a highly skilled programmer at least a month to complete. "Yesterday, I personally prompted AI to optimize a piece of code in about an hour," he wrote. According to Vembu, the AI not only understood the intended objective but also created a detailed execution plan, implemented the changes and generated extensive test cases on its own."The whole thing cost about $4 in tokens," he added.He also described how a non-technical colleague used a personal AI account to create a mechanical CAD design for a motor housing using newly released software, despite having no engineering background. Based on such experiences, Vembu concluded that AI is beginning to reshape intellectual professions in much the same way mechanisation transformed traditional manual trades. "What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers," he said.While highlighting the potential disruption, Vembu also pointed to what he sees as AI's democratising effect. He said his colleague's ability to perform engineering-related design work without formal training demonstrates how AI can empower people with curiosity and initiative to explore domains that were previously inaccessible."AI can enable a curious and active mind to explore realms he could not imagine doing before AI," Vembu wrote. The comments come as AI systems continue to demonstrate stronger capabilities in coding, mathematics, scientific research and engineering, fuelling debate over their impact on jobs and professional expertise.Vembu said he agreed with Prof Subbarao, whom he credited with extensive work evaluating AI capability, and reacted to the professor’s essay on whether AI is destroying humanity’s sense of purpose. That essay, part of a “Sunday Harangue” series, argues that every technological revolution destroys purpose for some group, as industrialization did for weavers and craftsmen. What may be different this time, it says, is the class of people affected. Intellectuals have rarely faced such a loss, and they are articulate about it, which would explain the heightened angst.The essay says mathematicians may be conflating the loss of purpose in their own lives with a loss of purpose for humanity. A weaver could rightly say finished cloth is only a fraction of the experience of making it, it notes, yet most people welcome cheap machine-made cloth and civilization advanced. Civilization, it suggests, may not end because humans are not the only ones doing math. It adds that the angst does not pass down generations. The children of displaced weavers found purpose native to the new world. The loss is real but “generation-bounded,” the essay argues, which underlies its optimism that humanity, if not every individual, finds “a new equation” after the dip.
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has drawn parallels between the impact of artificial intelligence on knowledge workers and the effect mechanisation had on traditional craftsmen during the industrial revolution. He said AI is beginning to reshape intellectual professions in much the same way mechanisation transformed traditional manual trades. The comments come as AI systems continue to demonstrate stronger capabilities.

Article Title: Mozilla to Apple: Why should we have to build Firefox twice for the iPhone
Article Text:
Why the browser engine matters

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What Apple’s browser choice screen can change

Mozilla has claimed that it would need to build Firefox twice. The browser maker says Apple ’s rules prevent it from bringing Gecko, the engine that powers Firefox on desktop and Android, to iPhone users through an update to the Firefox app they already have. The iPhone app currently uses WebKit, the same engine Apple uses in Safari.In a recent blog post, Mozilla said it would have to release Gecko in “a whole separate app, a second Firefox.” Existing users would then have to download that app, transfer their bookmarks, saved passwords and browsing history, and manually switch to it. Mozilla says those steps could deter people who already picked Firefox, including users who selected it from Apple’s browser choice screen in the European Union.A browser engine interprets a website’s code, draws the page on screen and runs scripts that make it interactive. Firefox on the iPhone has its own interface and account features, but WebKit handles the pages users open. On Windows, macOS and Android, Gecko does that work. Mozilla says some Firefox features are built into Gecko, which limits what it can bring to the iPhone while the app relies on WebKit.In 2024, Apple started allowing alternative engines in the EU under the Digital Markets Act, and soon thereafter, similar permissions were introduced in Japan with iOS 26.2.To use their own engine, developers need to get Apple’s approval. Apple says the terms are meant to protect users’ security and privacy, and developers have to promise to deliver timely security fixes. Its developer documentation also encourages breaking out things like page rendering and network traffic into their own components.In its March 2026 compliance report, Apple said browser makers can replace the WebKit version listed on the EU choice screen with a version that uses a different engine. That would let someone choosing Firefox from the screen download the Gecko app. Mozilla’s complaint concerns people who already have Firefox installed and would have to move to the new app themselves.Mozilla says millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iPhones has doubled since the EU began requiring Apple to offer a browser choice. The company says it has spent nearly three years testing Apple’s conditions and seeking changes. As of November 20, Mozilla said no developer had launched a non-WebKit browser under the rules in either the EU or Japan.
Article Summary: Mozilla says Apple’s rules prevent it from bringing Gecko, the engine that powers Firefox on desktop and Android, to iPhone users. The iPhone app currently uses WebKit, the same engine Apple uses in Safari. Existing users would have to download that app, transfer their bookmarks, saved passwords and browsing history, and manually switch to it.
